data.text/html:
Matrix Factorization: factoring the unfactorable

An interactive companion to Matrix Factorization – Numberphile with Prof. David Eisenbud. Some polynomials can't be factored. Mathematicians have handled stuck problems like this before: they enlarge the domain. Negative numbers, fractions, and i were all added this way. Dirac enlarged it to matrices, and Eisenbud proved that almost every polynomial can then be factored.

data.text/markdown:
1. Factoring, and why you sometimes need a bigger toolbox

The video opens with middle-school factoring: ||[x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2),\qquad x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y),\qquad x^2+2xy+y^2=(x+y)^2 .||]||(x^2+3||) will not factor over the rationals, because there is no square root of ||(-3||). "If you enlarge the domain of things you accept, there's a factorization." Allow complex numbers and ||(x^2+3=(x-i\sqrt3)(x+i\sqrt3)||). This is the same move that gave us fractions (to solve ||(3x-1=0||)) and negative numbers (to solve ||(3x+1=0||)). Pick a polynomial and a number system. Watch which factorizations appear and which never do.

data.text/html:
f = ||(x^{2} + 3||) → ||(x^{2} + 3||)

number system best factorization
integers / rationals ℚ ||(x^{2} + 3||) ❌ stuck
add square roots (√3) ||(x^{2} + 3||) ❌ stuck
add i as well (complex) ||(\left(x - \sqrt{3} i\right) \left(x + \sqrt{3} i\right)||) ✅ factors

It only splits once you allow \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(i||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(x^2+y^2||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e also needs \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(i||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||((x-iy)(x+iy)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNow pick \u003cstrong\u003eDirac's polynomial\u003c/strong\u003e \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(t^2+x^2+y^2+z^2||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e (and its cousin \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(xy-uv||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e). They stay stuck \u003cstrong\u003eeven with complex numbers\u003c/strong\u003e. No number system rescues them. That is the cliffhanger the rest of the lesson resolves.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2. How do you multiply matrices? Rows times columns

To factor into matrices we first need a matrix multiplication. Eisenbud writes it out for ||(2\times2||): ||[\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a'&b'\\c'&d'\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}aa'+bc' & ab'+bd'\\ ca'+dc' & cb'+dd'\end{pmatrix}.||]Each entry of the product is a row of the first matrix combined with a column of the second. Because rows and columns play different roles, order matters: in general ||(AB\neq BA||). "They don't commute." Drag the blue and orange numbers up or down. Hover a red entry to see the row and column that produce it.

data.text/markdown:
3. Dirac's trick: factor ||(xy-uv||) with matrices

Dirac's polynomial ||(t^2+x^2+y^2+z^2||) becomes, after a complex change of coordinates, the simpler-looking ||(xy-uv||). Ordinary polynomials can't factor it. With matrices it is one line: ||[ \color{#2e86de}{\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}x&u\\v&y\end{pmatrix}}_{A}}\; \color{#f18f01}{\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}y&-u\\-v&x\end{pmatrix}}_{B}} =\color{#e4572e}{\begin{pmatrix}xy-uv&0\\0&xy-uv\end{pmatrix}} = (xy-uv)\cdot I . ||]"This equality is wrong" if you read it literally, because the left side is a matrix and the right side a polynomial. The polynomial is personified as ||((xy-uv)||) times the identity matrix ||(I||), which behaves like the number 1. In that sense, ||(A\cdot B||) factors ||(xy-uv||). Plug in numbers and check that the product is always ||(f||) on the diagonal and zero elsewhere, in both orders.

data.text/html: ||[\color{#2e86de}{\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\4 & 2\end{matrix}\right]}\color{#f18f01}{\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1\\-4 & 3\end{matrix}\right]} = \color{#e4572e}{\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 0\\0 & 2\end{matrix}\right]}\qquad \color{#f18f01}{\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1\\-4 & 3\end{matrix}\right]}\color{#2e86de}{\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\4 & 2\end{matrix}\right]} = \color{#e4572e}{\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 0\\0 & 2\end{matrix}\right]}||]||(f = xy-uv = 3\cdot2 - 1\cdot4 = 2||). Symbolically, ||(AB - fI = \left[\begin{matrix}0 & 0\\0 & 0\end{matrix}\right]||) and ||(BA - fI = \left[\begin{matrix}0 & 0\\0 & 0\end{matrix}\right]||).

The product becomes the \u003cstrong\u003ezero matrix\u003c/strong\u003e, even though neither A nor B is zero. Ordinary numbers can't do that (\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(ab=0||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e forces \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(a=0||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e or \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(b=0||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNotice that \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(B||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e is just \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(A||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e with the diagonal swapped and the off-diagonal negated, its \u003cstrong\u003eadjugate\u003c/strong\u003e. And \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(xy-uv=\\det A||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. Hold on to that; the sandbox uses it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(AB||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e and \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(BA||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e agree here, unlike in Section 2. A matrix factorization requires \u003cstrong\u003eboth\u003c/strong\u003e \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(AB=fI||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e and \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(BA=fI||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4. Dirac wanted a square root: go up to 4×4

Dirac didn't just want a factorization. He wanted a square root, a single matrix ||(M||) with ||(M\cdot M = f\cdot I||). "This requires bigger matrices, no problem." Stack the two factors from Section 3 into a ||(4\times4||) block matrix: ||[M=\begin{pmatrix}0&\color{#2e86de}{A}\\ \color{#f18f01}{B}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad M^2=\begin{pmatrix}\color{#2e86de}{A}\color{#f18f01}{B}&0\\0&\color{#f18f01}{B}\color{#2e86de}{A}\end{pmatrix}=\color{#e4572e}{(xy-uv)\,I_4}.||]So ||(M||) is a square root of ||(xy-uv||). Here is the change of coordinates that turns Dirac's ||(t^2+x^2+y^2+z^2||) into this form:

With ||(x\to t+iz,\; y\to t-iz,\; u\to ix+y,\; v\to ix-y||): ||(\quad xy-uv \;\longrightarrow\; \color{#e4572e}{t^{2} + x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}||). Dirac's operator in disguise. (This is where complex numbers come in, as the video says.)

data.text/markdown:
5. Eisenbud's theorem: (almost) everything factors

"f = 1 · f" factors anything, but you learn nothing from it. So ban constants: no numbers alone in any matrix entry. Then degree counting blocks some polynomials. A product of entries with no constant term has degree ≥ 2, so a polynomial with a linear term like ||(x||) or ||(x+y^2||) is out.
Theorem (Eisenbud, 1980). Any polynomial with no constant and no linear term has a matrix factorization ||(A\,B = B\,A = f\cdot I||) in which no entry of ||(A||) or ||(B||) has a constant term.
"I can write down an algorithm which would produce the matrix factorization of whatever you want, or the machine will do it for me." Here is a simple version of such a machine:
  1. Every monomial has degree ≥ 2, so write ||(f = x_1 g_1 + x_2 g_2 + \dots + x_n g_n||), where each ||(g_i||) has no constant term.
  2. Start with the ||(1\times1||) factorization ||([x_1]\,[g_1]||).
  3. Add one term ||(x\,g||) at a time with the block rule ||(A' = \begin{pmatrix}A & xI\\ -gI & B\end{pmatrix},\; B' = \begin{pmatrix}B & -xI\\ gI & A\end{pmatrix}||), which doubles the size. Section 3 is exactly this rule applied to ||(xy + u(-v)||).
Type a polynomial, including Brady's ||(x^3+79y^2+34xz||):

data.text/markdown:
6. Another "matrix factorization": the recommender grid

The video ends with real-world uses. Outside pure maths, matrix factorization most often means something else, and you'd be using it every time Netflix suggests a film. Take a ratings matrix ||(R||) (users × movies, mostly blank) and approximate it by a product of two thin matrices: ||[\color{#e4572e}{R}\;\approx\;\color{#2e86de}{U}\,\color{#f18f01}{V^\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{\text{users}\times k},\; V\in\mathbb{R}^{\text{movies}\times k}.||]
Eisenbud / Dirac Recommender
entries polynomials real numbers
equality exact: ||(AB=f\,I||) approximate, fit only on the known cells
goal understand ||(f||) fill in the blanks: predict unseen ratings
Click cells to rate. The factors ||(U||) and ||(V||) are refit (alternating least squares) every time you click.

data.text/markdown:
7. Sandbox: every matrix is half of a factorization

The pattern behind Section 3: for any square matrix ||(A||), the adjugate ||(\operatorname{adj}(A)||) satisfies ||[A\cdot\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)\cdot A=\det(A)\,I .||]So any matrix of polynomials gives a matrix factorization of its determinant. Fill in a ||(2\times2||) or ||(3\times3||) matrix and see which polynomial you have factored. Matrices whose entries are all linear (as in Dirac's case) give the most interesting results.
